items.title: Home
items.text:
Drush is a command line shell and Unix scripting interface for Drupal. Drush adds commands to Drupal core's dr command line tool: database updates, deployments, SQL queries, config, users, roles, queues, and more.

Learn about the major changes in Drush 15.

items.title: Creating Custom Commands
items.text: Drush commands are plain Symfony Console commands, run by Drupal's dr. A module provides a command by adding a class; there is no Drush base class, and no Drush-specific registration. See Drush 15: The Doctor will see you now

items.title: Where commands live
items.text:
Put each command in its own class under the module's src/Command directory:

  • File: modules/custom/example/src/Command/XkcdFetchCommand.php
  • Namespace: Drupal\example\Command

Drupal finds every class in that directory that has an #[AsCommand] attribute, registers it as a service, and autowires its constructor. The module must be installed, and the container rebuilt (dr cc container) after you add a command.

items.title: Writing a command
items.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Drupal\example\Command;

use Drupal\Core\StringTranslation\StringTranslationTrait;
use GuzzleHttp\ClientInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Attribute\Argument;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Attribute\AsCommand;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Command\Command;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Output\OutputInterface;

/**
 * An example console command.
 *
 * Drupal discovers classes with #[AsCommand] in a module's src/Command
 * directory and autowires their constructor arguments. To try this one, copy it
 * to modules/example/src/Command/XkcdFetchCommand.php in a module named
 * 'example', enable the module, then run `dr xkcd random`.
 */
#[AsCommand(
    name: self::NAME,
    description: 'Display a link to an xkcd cartoon.',
    aliases: ['xkcd'],
    usages: [
        '123',
        'random',
    ],
)]
final class XkcdFetchCommand
{
    use StringTranslationTrait;

    public const string NAME = 'xkcd:fetch';

    public function __construct(
        private readonly ClientInterface $httpClient,
    ) {
    }

    public function __invoke(
        OutputInterface $output,
        #[Argument('A cartoon number, or "random". If omitted, the latest cartoon is used.')]
        string $search = '',
    ): int {
        $url = match (true) {
            $search === '' => 'https://xkcd.com',
            ctype_digit($search) => 'https://xkcd.com/' . $search,
            $search === 'random' => 'https://xkcd.com/' . random_int(1, $this->latestNumber()),
            default => throw new \InvalidArgumentException((string) $this->t('@search is not a cartoon number or "random".', ['@search' => $search])),
        };
        $output->writeln($url);
        return Command::SUCCESS;
    }

    /**
     * Returns the number of the most recent cartoon.
     */
    private function latestNumber(): int
    {
        $response = $this->httpClient->request('GET', 'https://xkcd.com/info.0.json');
        $info = json_decode((string) $response->getBody(), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
        return (int) $info['num'];
    }
}

The pieces:

  • The class is invokable: it has an __invoke() method and extends nothing. By convention its name ends in Command, and it declares public const string NAME holding the command name.
  • #[AsCommand] declares the name, description, aliases, usages, help, and hidden. Usages are shown after the command name, so write '123', not 'xkcd 123'.
  • Arguments and options are __invoke() parameters marked #[Argument] or #[Option]. The parameter type sets the input mode: a parameter with a default is optional, bool is a flag, and array accepts many values. Use suggestedValues for shell completion. Ask for InputInterface or OutputInterface as parameters when you need them.
  • Return Command::SUCCESS or Command::FAILURE, or an integer exit code. Throw an exception to report an error; Console prints it and exits non-zero.
  • User-facing strings go through StringTranslationTrait: (string) $this->t('Deleted @name.', ['@name' => $name]).

items.title: Dependency injection
items.text: Type-hint services in the constructor. Where a type hint is ambiguous, name the service with Symfony's #[Autowire(service: 'config.storage')] on the parameter. See Dependency Injection.

items.title: Prompting for input
items.text:
Mark an argument with #[Ask('Which queue?')] to prompt when it is missing. For anything more involved, such as autocompletion, add a method marked #[Interact]. It runs before __invoke(), and only when the command is interactive:

#[Interact]
public function askForName(InputInterface $input, OutputInterface $output): void
{
    if (empty($input->getArgument('config_name'))) {
        $question = new Question((string) $this->t('Choose a configuration'));
        $question->setAutocompleterValues($this->configFactory->listAll());
        $input->setArgument('config_name', (new SymfonyStyle($input, $output))->askQuestion($question));
    }
}

items.title: Exporting and Importing Configuration
items.text: Use config:export and config:import to move configuration between the database and files. Drupal core ships both commands from 12.1; on earlier versions Drush provides them.

items.title: Simple - value changes
items.text:
Per-environment value changes do not require exporting and importing configuration. Use Drupal's configuration override system instead.

The configuration override system allows you to change configuration values for a given instance of a site (e.g. the development server) by setting configuration variables in the site's settings.php file. For example, to change the name of a local development site: 

$config['system.site']['name'] = 'Local Install of Awesome Widgets, Inc.';
Note that the configuration override system is a Drupal feature, not a Drush feature. It should be the preferred method for changing configuration values on a per-environment basis; however, it does not work for some things, such as enabling and disabling modules.

items.title: Advanced - variation by environment
items.text:
• Drupal supports excluding development modules from enabling on higher environments.
  • See Config Split module for more advanced needs.

items.title: Dependency Injection
items.text:
A command gets the services it needs through its constructor. Drupal's container builds each command and autowires the constructor: each parameter's type hint names the service to inject.

public function __construct(
    private readonly EntityTypeManagerInterface $entityTypeManager,
    private readonly ConfigFactoryInterface $configFactory,
    #[Autowire(service: 'logger.channel.example')]
    private readonly LoggerInterface $logger,
) {
}
  • A type hint works when the container has a service or alias with that name. Core defines aliases for most of its interfaces, such as EntityTypeManagerInterface, ConfigFactoryInterface and GuzzleHttp\ClientInterface.
  • When a type has no alias, or several services share it, name the service with Symfony's #[Autowire(service: '...')] attribute (Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Attribute\Autowire), as above.
  • For a service from a module that may not be installed, make the parameter nullable with a null default. It receives null when the service is missing. EntitySaveCommand does this for content_moderation.

Don't call \Drupal::service() in a command. Injected services can be replaced in a test: build the command with new and pass what the test needs. See Testing.

items.title: Deploy
items.text:
10.3+

The deploy command standardizes how Drupal deployments work. The intent is your deployment script updates the codebase for the target site and then this command performs the following:

dr updatedb
dr config:import
dr cache:rebuild
dr deploy:hook
dr cache:warm

The steps run in one process, non-interactively, with their default options. If a step fails, the deployment stops.

items.title: Authoring update functions
items.text:
Below are the 3 types of update functions run by this command, in order. Choose the most appropriate for your need. Exercise caution when implementing HOOK_update_N() — the full API isn't available to you, see the documentation for more details.

Function Provided by Purpose HOOK_update_N() Drupal Low level changes. HOOK_post_update_NAME() Drupal Runs before config is imported. HOOK_deploy_NAME() Drush Runs after config is imported.

items.title: Customizing
items.text: deploy takes no options for its steps. If you need different options, run the steps yourself in your deployment script, in the order above.

items.title: Inspecting Drupal dependencies
items.text:
13.4+

These commands allow a developer or site builder to inspect the Drupal dependencies. It's similar with Composer's why command but acts in the Drupal realm, by showing dependencies between modules or config entities.

items.title: Find module dependants
items.text:
Drupal modules are able to define other modules as dependencies, using the module's metadata info.yml file. To get all modules that depend on a given module type:

dr why:module node --type=module

This will show all the installed module dependents of node module. The results are rendered visually as a tree, making it easy to understand the nested relations. It also marks visually the circular dependencies.

If you want to get the dependency tree as data, use the --format option. E.g., --format=yaml or --format=json.

The above command only rendered the dependency tree of installed modules. If you need to get the module dependants regardless whether they are installed or not, use the --no-only-installed option/flag:

dr why:module node --type=module --no-only-installed

Config entities are able to declare dependencies on modules. You can find also the config entities that depend on a given module. The following command shows all config entities depending on node module:

dr why:module node --type=config

Dependents are also rendered as a tree, showing a nested structure. The --format option can be used in the same way, to get a machine-readable structure.

items.title: Find config entity dependants
items.text:
Config entities are able also to declare dependencies on other config entities. With why:config we can determine the config entities depending on a specific entity:

dr why:config node.type.article

This will also render the results in a structured tree visualisation. Same, the --format option can be used to get data structured as json, yaml, etc.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Tip

Drush only supports one install method. It requires that your Drupal site be built with Composer and Drush be listed as a dependency.

  1. Composer. It is required that Drupal sites be built using Composer, with Drush listed as a dependency. See recommended-project (Drush must be added). If your Composer project doesn't yet depend on Drush, run composer require drush/drush to add it.
  2. Execution. Change to the project root, and call Drupal's vendor/bin/dr. To simplify things, add ./vendor/bin to your $PATH, allowing you to call dr from the project root. If you have only one Drupal codebase on your system, you may put /path/to/vendor/bin in your $PATH; now you can call dr from everywhere, without having to change to project root.
  3. Completion. Optional. Append to .bashrc or equivalent for ZSH or Fish shell. Run dr completion --help for more details.

Note

  • See Usage for details on using Drush.
  • To use a non-default PHP, edit ~/.bashrc so that the desired PHP is in front of your $PATH. If that is not desirable, you can change your PATH for just one request: PATH=/path/to/php:$PATH dr status ...
  • To use custom PHP configuration such as memory_limit, create a custom php.ini for Drush requests as per https://github.com/drush-ops/drush/issues/3294#issuecomment-370201342 and https://github.com/drush-ops/drush/issues/3294#issuecomment-618962852.
  • Porting commands from Drush 13? See Upgrading from Drush 13.

items.title: Events and Event Subscribers
items.text:
Tip

Drush hooks have been removed. Use event subscribers to change the behavior of other commands.

dr dispatches the standard Symfony Console events through Drupal's event_dispatcher service. Any module can subscribe to them, the same way it subscribes to Drupal's own events.

  • Symfony\Component\Console\Event\ConsoleCommandEvent (ConsoleEvents::COMMAND): runs before a command. Validate or adjust input, or call disableCommand() to stop it.
  • Symfony\Component\Console\Event\ConsoleErrorEvent (ConsoleEvents::ERROR): runs when a command throws.
  • Symfony\Component\Console\Event\ConsoleTerminateEvent (ConsoleEvents::TERMINATE): runs after a command completes.

items.title: Writing a subscriber
items.text:
Register the class as a service tagged event_subscriber in your module's *.services.yml:

services:
  example.console_subscriber:
    class: Drupal\example\EventSubscriber\ConsoleSubscriber
    tags:
      - { name: event_subscriber }

namespace Drupal\example\EventSubscriber;

use Symfony\Component\Console\ConsoleEvents;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Event\ConsoleCommandEvent;
use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\EventSubscriberInterface;

final class ConsoleSubscriber implements EventSubscriberInterface
{
    public static function getSubscribedEvents(): array
    {
        return [ConsoleEvents::COMMAND => 'onCommand'];
    }

    public function onCommand(ConsoleCommandEvent $event): void
    {
        if ($event->getCommand()?->getName() === 'sql:drop' && getenv('APP_ENV') === 'prod') {
            $event->getOutput()->writeln('sql:drop is disabled in production.');
            $event->disableCommand();
        }
    }
}

items.title: Events dispatched by Drush commands
items.text:
Commands may dispatch their own events by injecting Psr\EventDispatcher\EventDispatcherInterface. For example, cache:clear dispatches Drush\Event\CacheClearEvent; call its addType() to offer another cache type.

sql:sanitize does all of its work in subscribers. It dispatches Drush\Event\SanitizeConfirmsEvent to collect a summary, asks for confirmation once, and exits. A sanitizer subscribes to:

  • Drush\Event\SanitizeConfirmsEvent: call addMessage() to describe what will be done.
  • ConsoleEvents::TERMINATE: do the work, when the command is sql:sanitize and getExitCode() is 0.

The subscribers that ship with Drush are working examples. SanitizeSessionsSubscriber is the shortest.

items.title: Adding options to a command
items.text:
A ConsoleEvents::COMMAND subscriber may add options to a command's definition. Symfony binds and validates input after this event, so the new options are accepted on the command line. Add them whichever command is running, so that help, list and shell completion show them too. This is how sql:sanitize gets --sanitize-email and its other options; see SanitizeUserTableSubscriber and SanitizeOptionsTrait.

public function onCommand(ConsoleCommandEvent $event): void
{
    $application = $event->getCommand()?->getApplication();
    if (!$application?->has('sql:sanitize')) {
        return;
    }
    $command = $application->get('sql:sanitize');
    if (!$command->getNativeDefinition()->hasOption('example')) {
        $command->addOption('example', null, InputOption::VALUE_REQUIRED, 'An example option.');
    }
}

items.title: Usage
items.text:
Drush can be run in your shell by typing dr from within your project root directory or anywhere within Drupal.

$ dr [options] <command> [argument1] [argument2]

Use the help command to get a list of available options and commands:

$ dr help pm:list

Drush needs to be told the domain of your site in order for commands to generate correct links (e.g. user:login). You may set a DRUPAL_URI environment variable, or use the --url option.

$ dr --url=http://example.com user:login

items.title: Where commands come from
items.text:
dr belongs to Drupal core. Drush and your modules add commands to it.

flowchart LR
    dr["vendor/bin/dr"] --> core["Drupal core<br/>cache:rebuild, user:login, system:cron, ..."]
    dr --> drush["Drush<br/>updatedb, deploy, sql:*, config:get, ..."]
    dr --> mods["Your modules<br/>src/Command/*Command.php"]

Run dr list to see what is available on your site. The list depends on the site's state:

  • Before Drupal is installed, Drush adds only commands that need no installed site, such as sql:cli and php:eval.
  • Some Drush commands appear only when their module is installed: watchdog:* (dblog), image:* (image), jn:get (jsonapi), workspace:publish (workspaces).
  • When Drupal core ships a command, Drush steps aside and core's version runs. This applies to config:export, config:import, ex:install and ex:uninstall on newer core versions.

items.title: sql:dump
items.text:
Export the Drupal DB as SQL using mysqldump or equivalent.

Without --result-file the dump is written to standard output. With it, the path of the file is printed, as plain text or with --format as json or yaml, so that a caller can find the dump. There is no automatic file naming; let the shell build a dated path, as in the examples.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• sql:dump --result-file=../18.sql
  • sql:dump --result-file=$HOME/drush-backups/$(date -I).sql --gzip
  • sql:dump --skip-tables-list=cache*,sessions,watchdog
  • sql:dump --structure-tables-list=cache*,sessions --result-file=../18.sql --format=json
  • sql:dump --extra-dump=--no-data

items.title: Options
items.text:
• --result-file=RESULT-FILE. Save to a file instead of writing the dump to standard output. A relative path is relative to the Drupal root.
  • --create-db. Omit DROP TABLE statements. Used by Postgres only, when importing into a freshly created database.
  • --data-only. Dump data without statements to create any of the schema.
  • --ordered-dump. Order by primary key and add line breaks for efficient diffs. Slows down the dump. Mysql only.
  • --gzip. Compress the dump using the gzip program which must be in your $PATH.
  • --extra-dump=EXTRA-DUMP. Add custom arguments/options to the dumping of the database (e.g. mysqldump command).
  • --skip-tables-list=SKIP-TABLES-LIST. A comma-separated list of tables to exclude completely. Wildcards (*) are allowed.
  • --structure-tables-list=STRUCTURE-TABLES-LIST. A comma-separated list of tables to include for structure, but not data. Wildcards (*) are allowed.
  • --tables-list=TABLES-LIST. A comma-separated list of tables to transfer. Wildcards (*) are allowed.
  • --format=FORMAT. Print the path of the dump file as json or yaml. [possible values: yaml, json]

Modules may add their own operations with an event subscriber (a service tagged event_subscriber) that listens to: - Drush\Event\SanitizeConfirmsEvent: add a line to the summary shown before confirmation. - ConsoleEvents::TERMINATE: run queries or call APIs to sanitize, when the command is sql:sanitize and its exit code is 0. - ConsoleEvents::COMMAND: optionally, add options to this command. See https://www.drush.org/latest/subscribers/. Working subscribers are at https://github.com/drush-ops/drush/tree/15.x/src/EventSubscriber/sanitize

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• sql:sanitize --sanitize-password=no
  • sql:sanitize --allowlist-fields=field_biography,field_phone_number

items.title: Options
items.text:
• --sanitize-email=SANITIZE-EMAIL. The pattern for test email addresses in the sanitization operation, or no to keep email addresses unchanged. May contain replacement patterns %uid, %mail or %name. [default: user+%uid@localhost.localdomain]
  • --sanitize-password=SANITIZE-PASSWORD. By default, passwords are randomized. Specify no to disable that. Specify any other value to set all passwords to that value.
  • --ignored-roles=IGNORED-ROLES. A comma delimited list of roles. Users with at least one of the roles will be exempt from sanitization.
  • --allowlist-fields=ALLOWLIST-FIELDS. A comma delimited list of fields exempt from sanitization.

items.title: Guidelines
items.text: Drush is built by people like you! Please join us.

items.title: Git and Pull requests
items.text:
• Contributions are submitted, reviewed, and accepted using GitHub pull requests.
  • The latest changes are in the 15.x branch. PR's should initially target this branch.
  • See the test-specific README.md for instructions on running the test suite. Test before you push. Optionally run tests in the provided Docker containers.
  • We maintain branches named 15.x, 13.x, etc. These are release branches. From these branches, we make new tags for patch and minor versions.

items.title: Development Environment
items.text:
• You may choose to use the DDEV for a standardized development environment.
  • See composer run-script -l for a list of helper scripts.

items.title: Coding style
items.text:
• Do write comments. You don't have to comment every line, but if you come up with something that's a bit complex/weird, just leave a comment. Bear in mind that you will probably leave the project at some point and that other people will read your code. Undocumented huge amounts of code are nearly worthless!
  • We use PSR-12.
  • Keep it compatible. Do not introduce changes to the public API, or configurations too casually. Don't make incompatible changes without good reasons!
  • Run composer cs to check the project for coding style issues and run composer cbf to fix them automatically where possible. These scripts use PHP_CodeSniffer in background.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
• The docs are on our web site.
  • The site is built with Zensical. To preview it, run composer mk:docs to generate the command pages, install Zensical in a virtual environment (python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install zensical; needs Python 3.11+), then run .venv/bin/zensical serve.
  • Documentation should be kept up-to-date. This means, when you add or change a command, option, or event, update the docs in the same pull request.

items.title: Unish
items.text: Drush's command tests extend Drupal core's KernelTestBase. They instantiate a Symfony Console CommandTester object as is typical. See CircleCi.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
1. git clone https://github.com/drush-ops/drush.git
  2. cd drush
  3. composer install
  4. Set UNISH_DB_URL for the kernel suite, for example sqlite://localhost/:memory:?module=sqlite.
  5. Run all test suites: composer test

items.title: DDEV
items.text:
Drush's own tests may be run within provided Docker containers via DDEV. It sets UNISH_DB_URL for you.

  • Start containers: ddev start
  • Run a test: ddev exec composer kernel -- --filter testUserRole
  • See the DDEV's XDebug docs for help on enabling Xdebug.

items.title: Advanced usage
items.text:
• Run only one test suite
    • composer unit
    • composer kernel
  • Run only tests matching a regex: composer kernel -- --filter testUserRole
  • XML results: composer kernel -- --log-junit results.xml

items.title: About the Test Suites
items.text:
• Unit tests operate on functions that take values and return results without creating side effects. No database connection is required to run these tests, and no Drupal site is set up. They are configured in tests/phpunit.xml.dist.
  • Kernel tests extend Drupal core's KernelTestBase and drive a command directly with Symfony's CommandTester, the way Drupal core tests its own console commands. They run from tests/phpunit.kernel.xml.dist, whose bootstrap chains core's test bootstrap and derives SIMPLETEST_DB from UNISH_DB_URL. Each test gets a fresh, minimal Drupal with only the modules it lists. A class marked #[ShareEnvironment] builds that Drupal once, in setUpEnvironment(), and its test methods share the database; see the change record. QueueTest is a good model, both for Drush's own commands and for commands that ship in your module.

items.title: XkcdFetchCommand.php
items.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Drupal\example\Command;

use Drupal\Core\StringTranslation\StringTranslationTrait;
use GuzzleHttp\ClientInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Attribute\Argument;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Attribute\AsCommand;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Command\Command;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Output\OutputInterface;

/**
 * An example console command.
 *
 * Drupal discovers classes with #[AsCommand] in a module's src/Command
 * directory and autowires their constructor arguments. To try this one, copy it
 * to modules/example/src/Command/XkcdFetchCommand.php in a module named
 * 'example', enable the module, then run `dr xkcd random`.
 */
#[AsCommand(
    name: self::NAME,
    description: 'Display a link to an xkcd cartoon.',
    aliases: ['xkcd'],
    usages: [
        '123',
        'random',
    ],
)]
final class XkcdFetchCommand
{
    use StringTranslationTrait;

    public const string NAME = 'xkcd:fetch';

    public function __construct(
        private readonly ClientInterface $httpClient,
    ) {
    }

    public function __invoke(
        OutputInterface $output,
        #[Argument('A cartoon number, or "random". If omitted, the latest cartoon is used.')]
        string $search = '',
    ): int {
        $url = match (true) {
            $search === '' => 'https://xkcd.com',
            ctype_digit($search) => 'https://xkcd.com/' . $search,
            $search === 'random' => 'https://xkcd.com/' . random_int(1, $this->latestNumber()),
            default => throw new \InvalidArgumentException((string) $this->t('@search is not a cartoon number or "random".', ['@search' => $search])),
        };
        $output->writeln($url);
        return Command::SUCCESS;
    }

    /**
     * Returns the number of the most recent cartoon.
     */
    private function latestNumber(): int
    {
        $response = $this->httpClient->request('GET', 'https://xkcd.com/info.0.json');
        $info = json_decode((string) $response->getBody(), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
        return (int) $info['num'];
    }
}

items.title: git-bisect.sh
items.text:
#!/usr/bin/env sh

#
# Git bisect is a helpful way to discover which commit an error
# occurred in.  This example file gives simple instructions for
# using git bisect with Drush to quickly find erroneous commits
# in Drush commands or Drupal modules, presuming that you can
# trigger the error condition via Drush (e.g. using `dr php:eval`).
#
# Follow these simple steps:
#
#   $ git bisect start
#   $ git bisect bad              # Tell git that the current commit does not work
#   $ git bisect good bcadd5a     # Tell git that commit bcadd5a worked fine
#   $ git bisect run mytestscript.sh
#
# 'git bisect run' will continue to call 'git bisect good' and 'git bisect bad',
# based on whether the script's exit code was 0 or 1, respectively.
#
# Replace 'mytestscript.sh' in the example above with a custom script that you
# write yourself.  Use the example script at the end of this document as a
# guide.  Replace the example command with one that calls the Drush command
# that you would like to test, and replace the 'grep' string with a value
# that appears when the error exists in the commit, but does not appear when
# commit is okay.
#
# If you are using Drush to test Drupal or a module, and the command
# exits non-zero when there is a problem, use:
#
#   $ git bisect run dr mycommand
#
# If you need to test for an error condition explicitly, use the php:eval
# command to throw an exception when `myfunction()` returns FALSE. Replace
# 'myfunction()' with the name of an appropriate function in your module that
# can be used to detect the error condition you are looking for.
#
#   $ git bisect run dr php:eval 'if (!myfunction()) { throw new \Exception("ERR"); }'
#
dr mycommand --myoption 2>&1 | grep -q 'string that indicates there was a problem'
if [ $? == 0 ] ; then
  exit 1
else
  exit 0
fi
